title: Insalata Caprese
subtitle: Tomatoes and mozzarella with basil and olive oil
excerpt: The simplest and most famous Italian salad: alternating slices of ripe tomatoes and fresh mozzarella, scattered with basil leaves, and dressed only with the best olive oil and a little sea salt. Everything depends on the quality of the ingredients.

recipe.sourceNotes: Insalata caprese takes its name from the island of Capri, where the combination of tomato, mozzarella, and basil is thought to have originated, perhaps as a representation of the Italian flag. The dish became internationally famous in the twentieth century as Italian cuisine spread beyond Italy's borders and as buffalo mozzarella became more widely available outside Campania. Its simplicity is both its greatest quality and its most demanding requirement: every component must be excellent. A caprese made with out-of-season supermarket tomatoes and rubbery industrial mozzarella is a pale shadow of one made with ripe, sun-warmed summer tomatoes and fresh buffalo mozzarella. No balsamic vinegar: the modern British habit of drizzling balsamic over caprese is not traditional and overwhelms the delicate mozzarella.

content.text: Use the ripest, most flavourful tomatoes available. In summer, outdoor-grown heritage or beef tomatoes are ideal. Buffalo mozzarella from Campania has a more complex flavour and a softer, creamier texture than regular cow's-milk mozzarella; use it if you can. Dress only with the best extra-virgin olive oil, fruity rather than grassy. No balsamic vinegar: it overpowers everything else.

items.preparation: fresh buffalo mozzarella; drained and sliced about 7 mm thick

content.text: Arrange alternating slices of tomato and mozzarella on a flat plate or platter, slightly overlapping or in a single layer, in whatever pattern looks best. Tuck whole basil leaves between and on top of the slices.

Season with sea salt and black pepper. Drizzle the olive oil generously over the top. Serve immediately at room temperature; never chilled. Mozzarella served cold from the fridge loses its milky flavour and becomes rubbery.
